8. Expectations and responsibilities

All workers are expected to take personal responsibility for observing, upholding, promoting, and applying this policy. Regardless of position or seniority, every individual has a duty to contribute to a respectful, inclusive, and safe working environment. Commitment to these principles is an integral part of everyone’s role within UKAEA and is essential to fostering a positive and collaborative workplace culture.

Any dealings workers have with third parties, including customers, suppliers, contractors, agency staff and consultants, must be free from harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination or victimisation.

All workers are advised to be mindful of their behaviour at all times and consider how this may be perceived by others. Conduct may constitute as harassment regardless of the individual’s intention or motive. What one person may consider a ‘joke’ can be offensive to another. Furthermore, a single action can amount to harassment if it is sufficiently serious.

All workers may be held personally liable for acts of discrimination and/or harassment. Personal liability means that individuals can be held legally and disciplinarily responsible for their behaviour, regardless of whether it was committed intentionally or negligently. This includes conduct that violates this policy, or applicable laws related to discrimination, harassment, bullying or victimisation.

If any individual experiences or witnesses any form harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination or victimisation they are strongly encouraged to report it promptly to their line manager or a member of the People and Culture team. Early reporting helps ensure that appropriate support and action can be taken in a timely manner.

8.1 How complaints and allegations will be managed

Complaints and allegations of harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination, or victimisation may be raised in several ways: informally, formally, or anonymously. Further guidance on how to raise a concern can be found in the supporting documents.

All allegations raised through the formal procedure will be investigated thoroughly and addressed under the relevant Grievance Policy and / or Disciplinary Policy and Procedure. Where behaviour is found to constitute gross misconduct, this may result in disciplinary action up to and including summary dismissal (dismissal without notice).

The UKAEA is committed to handling all complaints and allegations in an impartial, fair, and timely manner. In doing so, we will:

ensure all formal complaints are investigated promptly, thoroughly, and impartially

protect the dignity, rights, and wellbeing of all parties involved, including complainants, respondents, and witnesses, ensuring that no individual is subject to unfair treatment or retaliation

ensure that investigating managers act with the highest standards of professionalism, fairness, and discretion. All concerns will be listened to respectfully, without bias, judgement, or minimisation

adopt a compassionate, people-centred approach and provide appropriate support to those involved, including access to employee support services where required

ensure that investigations and outcomes are progressed without unnecessary delay, balancing the need for thoroughness with the importance of timely resolution

ensure investigations and outcomes take into account any aggravating factors, such as an abuse of power or authority over a more junior colleague

8.2 How third-party complaints and allegations will be managed

Where the alleged bully or harasser is a third party (for example, a contractor, client, or visitor), the procedure outlined in this policy may need to be adapted to reflect the circumstances. In such cases, UKAEA will take reasonable steps to ensure that a fair and thorough investigation is conducted, liaising with the relevant third party or their employer where appropriate to address the matter. If any allegation of harassment by a third-party proves to be well-founded, steps taken by UKAEA may include warning the individual about the inappropriate nature of their behaviour, banning the individual from UKAEA premises, reporting individual actions to the individual’s employer and/or relevant authorities including the police.

8.3 Support for those affected or involved

It is recognised that anyone affected by, or involved in, a complaint of bullying or harassment may feel anxious, distressed, or uncertain about what will happen next. UKAEA are committed to providing appropriate support and ensuring that everyone involved is treated with empathy and respect throughout the process.

If an employee feels unable to continue working in close contact with the alleged bully or harasser, UKAEA will give careful and compassionate consideration to any requests for temporary adjustments to working arrangements while the matter is under investigation.

Employees can access free, confidential emotional support through the Employee Assistance Programme (EAP). Details can be found on Nucleus. In addition, employees may wish to seek support from a member of the People and Culture Team, internal staff networks or our team of Mental Health First Aiders, who will be able to signpost to further support. Members of our recognised trade union can also contact their union representative for advice and support throughout the process.

Issue 1 - September 2026

1. Purpose and scope

The purpose of this policy is to affirm that all workers have the right to work in an environment where they are treated with dignity, respect and fairness. Any form of harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination or victimisation are unacceptable forms of behaviour at UKAEA and will not be permitted, condoned, or tolerated under any circumstances.

If any individual is found to have committed, authorised, or condoned an act of bullying, harassment or discrimination, UKAEA will take appropriate and proportionate action in accordance with our Disciplinary Procedure. This may include, where applicable, disciplinary measures up to and including summary dismissal. In the case of contractors or third parties, such behaviour may result in termination of engagement or other appropriate contractual remedies.

This policy applies to all individuals working for or engaged by UKAEA, including employees, contractors, agency workers, consultants, and apprentices. It also applies to job applicants and is relevant at every stage of the employment lifecycle.

The policy extends to all workplace interactions and environments, whether taking place on UKAEA premises, at off-site locations, or in virtual or hybrid working settings. It also applies to work-related social activities, training events, conferences, and business travel.

This policy extends to the use of social media and other online platforms where individuals are identifiable as being associated with UKAEA, or where the content visible has a clear connection to their role or activities within the organisation.

In addition, the policy covers instances of harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination, victimisation or other forms of inappropriate behaviour carried out by third parties, such as customers, suppliers, visitors, or other stakeholders with whom UKAEA workers may come into contact in the course of their work.

2. Definitions

2.1 Harassment

Harassment is defined as unwanted behaviour related to a protected characteristic and is unlawful. Harassment, under the Equality Act 2010, has the purpose or effect of:

violating someone else’s dignity

creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment for someone else

Harassment can also occur in the following circumstances:

perception - where a person is subjected to harassment because they are perceived to have a protected characteristic, even if that perception is incorrect

association – where a person is harassed because of their association with someone who has a protected characteristic

The key factor is how the behaviour is experienced by the recipient. Conduct that may seem trivial or harmless to one person may have a profound impact on another. All workers are therefore expected to exercise sensitivity, professionalism, and respect in their interactions.

Under the Equality Act 2010, there are nine protected characteristics. These are:

age

disability

gender reassignment

marriage or civil partnership

pregnancy and maternity

race

sexual orientation

religion or belief

sex

2.2 Examples of harassment

Harassment can take many forms. It may be verbal, non-verbal, written, physical, or online, and can occur in person, via email, telephone, messaging platforms, or social media. Examples include (but are not limited to):

Verbal

Offensive jokes, comments, or ‘banter’ about someone’s protected characteristic; derogatory terms or name-calling; mocking accents, appearance, or abilities; unwelcome remarks about a person’s body, dress, or private life.

Non-verbal

Displaying offensive images, posters, or gestures that target a protected characteristic; using facial expressions or body language to demean someone because of a protected characteristic.

Physical

Unwanted touching, pushing, or other physical contact connected to a protected characteristic; intimidating body language or gestures; invading personal space in a way that targets someone’s protected characteristic.

Written or digital

Sending offensive emails, texts, or social media messages related to a protected characteristic; circulating inappropriate images, memes, or rumours about a colleague because of a protected characteristic; deliberately excluding someone from work-related communications or groups due to a protected characteristic.

Sexual

Sexual harassment is unwanted behaviour of a sexual nature, and does not need to be related to a protected characteristic. More information can be found in the following section.

Harassment by perception or association

Teasing, isolating, or discriminating against someone because they are perceived to have a protected characteristic, even if inaccurate; harassing an individual because of their association with someone who has a protected characteristic (for example: family member, partner, or friend).

2.3 Sexual harassment

Sexual harassment is a form of harassment that is sexual in nature. Sexual harassment is unlawful and under the Equality Act 2010, it is defined as:

conduct of a sexual nature that has the purpose or effect of:

violating an individual’s dignity

creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating, or offensive environment

less favourable treatment related to sex or gender reassignment that occurs because of a rejection of, or submission to, sexual conduct

2.4 Examples of sexual harassment

Sexual harassment can take many forms and may occur at work, outside work, in person, or online. It may involve a single incident or a series of incidents. Importantly, sexual harassment is determined by how the behaviour is perceived by the recipient, not by the intent of the person engaging in the conduct, and can affect any individual regardless of their position, gender, or relationship to the perpetrator. Examples include (but are not limited to):

Verbal
